name: Sooke

recheck.scope: facts left unverified because www.sooke.ca was blocked

facts.text: We could not confirm from the District's website whether Sooke has a tree-cutting bylaw for private land; a 2020 news report says the District surveyed residents on a proposed tree management bylaw. Check with the District of Sooke (250-642-1634) before removing large trees. Trees on District boulevards, parks and trails fall under Policy 11.6 (see sooke-municipal-trees-policy). Inside development permit areas (foreshore, riparian, steep slopes and others), vegetation removal is regulated through the OCP; see sooke-ocp-800-dpas.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke survey collects thoughts on tree bylaw - Sooke News Mirror
facts.excerpt: Sooke council is working on a bylaw to regulate tree management.
facts.note: V3 STILL UNVERIFIED (status note, NOT a claim that no bylaw exists). Re-checked on www.sooke.ca, now allowed: the Bylaws page lists Burning, Noise, Parking and Securing Attractants regulation pages and no tree page. The 'Browse and Search Bylaws' list is filled by a script that calls a /umbraco/ endpoint, which the site's robots.txt disallows, so it was not queried. The District's public sitemap (https://www.sooke.ca/sitemap.xml, 744 URLs, read 2026-11-21) lists 78 bylaw pages; none has 'tree' in its title. The only tree document listed is 'Trees On Municipal Property (Policy No. 11.6)', adopted January 24, 2005, which covers boulevards, parks and trails only. A sitemap is not a complete register, so this is NOT evidence that no bylaw exists. The 2020 news article (SECONDARY) still could not be re-fetched (www.sookenewsmirror.com is not allowed). Earlier (V2): the Urban Forest and Tree Care page gives care advice and describes no tree-cutting permit; that is still true on www.sooke.ca.

facts.text: Sooke's Policy 11.6 (2005) covers trees on District boulevards, parks and trails. A request to trim or remove a municipal tree for a better view is reviewed by the Municipal Engineer, who may allow trimming; removal must be authorized by Council, and the applicant bears all costs and liabilities. Trees the District considers dangerous are removed by its own tree contractor.
facts.sourceTitle: Trees on Municipal Property: Boulevards, Parks and Trails (Policy No. 11.6, District of Sooke, adopted January 24, 2005)
facts.excerpt: Removal of these trees must be authorized by Council. All costs and liabilities arising from this action are to be borne by the applicant.
facts.note: V3: NEW, found while re-checking sooke-tree-bylaw-status. Listed at https://www.sooke.ca/media-manager/media-pages/policies/trees-on-municipal-property-policy-no-116/. Same PDF, verbatim: 'The Municipal Engineer may grant permission for the trimming of these trees.' and 'Trees, which are felt to be dangerous to the public by the District of Sooke, are to be removed by the District of Sooke tree contractor.' Applies to municipal property only; it says nothing about trees on private land.

facts.text: Most of Sooke's tree canopy is on private land. The District's tree-care guidance tells owners to water young trees for their first 2-3 years, prune dead or damaged branches ideally in the dormant season, and hire a certified arborist for large or complex work.
facts.sourceTitle: Urban Forest and Tree Care - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Most of Sooke’s tree canopy is on private land.
facts.note: V2: new. Same page, verbatim: 'Hire a certified arborist for large or complex work.' Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network). V3: re-opened on www.sooke.ca on 2026-11-21 (the host is now allowed); the excerpt matches the live page.

facts.text: Sooke is a forested community, and the District's FireSmart landscaping advice is to keep 1-1.5 m of non-combustible space around the home, keep shrubs and woody debris tidy and well spaced from 1.5 to 10 m out, prune branches up to 2 m from the ground, and keep trees at least 10 m from structures where possible. Sooke Fire Rescue Services (250-642-5422) books free home and property assessments.
facts.sourceTitle: Urban Forest and Tree Care - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Call Sooke Fire Rescue Services at 250-642-5422 to book a free home and property assessment.

facts.text: Sooke adopted Official Community Plan Bylaw No. 800 on December 8, 2025. Its Part 7 sets out nine development permit areas: Energy and Water, General, Foreshore Area, Riparian Area, Steep Slopes, Town Centre, Intensive Residential, Neighbourhood Commercial and Employment Lands. Inside them, land alteration, building and subdivision need a development permit unless an exemption applies, and a DPA Viewer map shows which may apply to a property.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: issuance of a Development Permit is required prior to any proposed land alteration, building and subdivision within a DPA.
facts.note: V2: Correction: the adopted plan has NINE DPAs (DPA 1-9), not the '10 DPAs' Capital Daily reported for the DRAFT. The OCP page (https://www.sooke.ca/programs-services/planning-and-development/official-community-plan-ocp/), verbatim: 'On December 8, 2025, Council adopted Official Community Plan (OCP) Bylaw No. 800 (PDF)'. There is no separate wildfire DPA; Part 7 can require a wildfire hazard assessment for lands over 4 ha. The PDF was fetched from the District's Govstack media host, the same host as the earlier sourceUrl. V3: the OCP page now opens on www.sooke.ca and still carries the adoption sentence; the Part 7 PDF re-opened on the Govstack media host.

facts.text: Sooke's OCP exempts yard or garden work within an existing landscaped area from development permits. It also exempts planting native trees, shrubs or groundcover to improve habitat or soil stability, and removing invasive plants (such as gorse, Scotch broom, knotweed, English ivy and daphne) by low-disturbance hand or mechanical methods, as long as native plants go back in right away.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: Yard or garden work within an existing landscaped area;
facts.note: V2: new (s.7.1.2 xiv, xv, xvii). The invasive-removal exemption, verbatim, requires 'immediate replacement with vegetation native to the surrounding ecosystem'.

facts.text: In Sooke's permit areas, removing hazardous trees is exempt only with an ISA Certified Arborist's report accepted by the District beforehand. In riparian and foreshore areas, the removal must also be supervised or confirmed by a Qualified Environmental Professional.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: In riparian or foreshore Development Permit Areas, hazardous tree removal must be supervised or confirmed by a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP)

facts.text: Sooke's Foreshore Area permit area deals with grading, vegetation removal or structural works within about 15 m of the sea's natural boundary. It is not meant to regulate routine maintenance or gardening in existing yards, and its guidelines ask that existing trees and native vegetation be kept within at least 15 m upland of the shore.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: The intent is not to regulate routine property maintenance, gardening, or enjoyment of existing residential yards
facts.note: V2: new (s.7.4.1 and guideline viii, 'Retain existing trees and native vegetation within a minimum of 15 metres upland').

facts.text: Sooke's Steep Slopes permit area (DPA 5) covers mapped parcels and any land with slopes over 30% across at least 10 m horizontally. Land clearing and other site disturbance there is reviewed to protect slope stability and properties downhill.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: have slopes greater than 30% for a minimum horizontal distance of 10m.

facts.text: Backyard burning in Sooke is allowed only from November 1 to April 30, when the ventilation index is Good, no fire ban is in place and the weather is safe. Under Fire Protection Services Bylaw No. 292, burning yard waste or clearing land needs a permit from Sooke Fire Rescue, and fires must be at least 15 m from buildings and property lines. As an alternative, the District runs free yard-waste drop-off in May at the Sooke Parks Yard, 2070 Kaltasin Road.
facts.excerpt: Backyard burning is permitted in the District of Sooke from November 1 to April 30, when ventilation is GOOD and conditions are safe.
facts.note: V2: the source is now the official District page, replacing the SECONDARY Island Social Trends post; the season dates are confirmed. Added from the page FAQ, verbatim: 'open burning beyond small recreational fires—including yard waste burning, land clearing, or larger fires—requires a permit issued by Sooke Fire Rescue.' The page's opening text and its FAQ differ on whether basic backyard burning needs a permit; tell readers to call Sooke Fire Rescue first. V3: re-opened on www.sooke.ca on 2026-11-21 (the host is now allowed); the excerpt matches the live page. For the drop-off rules (no commercial loads, no invasive plants), see sooke-yard-waste-dropoff.

facts.text: Sooke's priority invasive plants include knotweed, English ivy, Himalayan blackberry, Scotch broom, gorse, giant hogweed and garden escapees such as lamium, daphne and periwinkle. The District works with the T'Sou-ke Nation on knotweed along salmon streams and warns never to cut or compost knotweed or to compost any invasive plant.
facts.excerpt: Do not cut or compost: Cutting promotes regrowth and spreads fragments.
facts.note: V2: new official replacement for the invasive-species angle of sooke-scotch-broom. facts.text: Scotch broom is said to have reached Vancouver Island through an 1851 Sooke garden, and it still crowds rural Sooke lots.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke wants you to pull some broom - Times Colonist (May 5, 2024)
facts.excerpt: Sooke wants you to pull some broom
facts.note: V3 STILL UNVERIFIED: SECONDARY and not re-fetched (www.pressreader.com is not allowed). Re-checked on www.sooke.ca: no District page mentions 1851. CORRECTED: the old clause 'the District has run an annual broom drop-off at its parks yard' was REMOVED, because the District's 2026 free yard-waste drop-off does NOT accept invasive plant material (see sooke-yard-waste-dropoff). Use sooke-priority-invasives for broom, and the CRD Hartland rule (regional-crd-invasive-disposal) for disposal.

facts.text: Sooke runs a free yard-waste drop-off at the District Parks Yard, 2070 Kaltasin Road, for District residential owners and occupants: in May and, in 2026, also on Saturdays in October (the last 2026 day was October 31). It takes leaves, grass clippings, branches, prunings and garden debris, but not commercial loads or invasive plant material.
facts.sourceTitle: Final Free Yard Waste Drop-Off Day Set for October 31 (2026 Program) - District of Sooke (Oct 30, 2026)
facts.excerpt: Commercial loads and invasive plant materials cannot be accepted.
facts.note: V3: NEW, found while re-checking sooke-scotch-broom. Same bulletin, verbatim: 'The service is available to District of Sooke residential property owners and occupants.' September 3, 2026 bulletin (https://www.sooke.ca/news-and-public-notices/posts/free-yard-waste-drop-off-expands-to-october-as-sooke-firesmart-efforts-continue/), verbatim: 'Every Saturday in October, excluding Thanksgiving weekend'. The Burning Regulations page still describes the program as 'during the month of May'. TIME-BOUND: dates change yearly. A landscaping company's loads are commercial, so RNC cannot use this drop-off.

facts.text: The District says bears, cougars, deer, raccoons and other wildlife commonly move through Sooke neighbourhoods, especially in spring and fall. Gardens and fruit trees draw them in, and deer need space in fawning season.
facts.sourceTitle: Coexisting with Wildlife - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: It’s common to see bears, cougars, deer, raccoons, and other wildlife moving through neighbourhoods, especially in spring and fall.
facts.note: V2: new; closes the R1b deer gap for Sooke (no deer-management program found, just the District's guidance). facts.text: Sooke's Animal Regulation and Impounding Bylaw No. 392 requires residents to secure wildlife attractants, which it says include compost, fruit trees and fallen fruit. The District advises harvesting fruit promptly, clearing fallen fruit, and fencing or netting where appropriate.
facts.excerpt: Under Bylaw No. 392, residents must ensure attractants are secured.

facts.text: Sooke is on the CRD's Juan de Fuca water system (see regional-crd-water-systems), but some rural properties beyond the mains are reported to rely on wells or hauled water, and council has backed extending service to about 75 Otter Point Road properties. Confirm a property's supply before planning irrigation.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke council backs water service extension - Sooke News Mirror
facts.excerpt: Sooke council backed extending municipal water to about 75 properties on Otter Point Road
facts.note: V3 STILL UNVERIFIED: the District's sitemap (read 2026-11-21) has no page on the Otter Point Road water extension, wells or hauled water, and www.sookenewsmirror.com is still not allowed. Only the Juan de Fuca part is verified (regional-crd-water-systems). The excerpt is a search snippet and is undated.

facts.text: The District of Sooke notes that fall and winter storms bring higher tides, strong winds and storm surges to Sooke's coastline, washing driftwood, seaweed and debris onto the Whiffin Spit trail.
facts.sourceTitle: Storm Surges and High Tides Bring Seasonal Changes to Whiffin Spit - District of Sooke (Nov 16, 2026)
facts.excerpt: As fall and winter storms bring higher tides, strong winds and storm surges to Sooke's coastline
